by Immanuel Kant
translated by Thomas Kingsmill Abbott
PREFACE

Ancient Greek philosophy was divided into three sciences: physics, ethics, and logic. This division suits the nature of the subject perfectly. The only improvement we can make is to add the principle on which the division rests, so that we can confirm its completeness and identify its necessary subdivisions correctly.

All rational knowledge is either material or formal. Formal knowledge deals only with the form of understanding and reason itself, with the universal laws of thought, regardless of what those thoughts are about. Material knowledge deals with specific objects and the laws that govern them. Formal philosophy is called logic. Material philosophy, which concerns definite objects and the laws to which they are subject, splits in two: the laws are either laws of nature or laws of freedom. The science of the first is physics, the science of the second is ethics. They are also called natural philosophy and moral philosophy.

Logic cannot have any empirical part — that is, no part where the universal and necessary laws of thought would rest on grounds drawn from experience. Otherwise it would not be logic at all, but only a fallible record of how people happen to think. A canon for understanding and reason, valid for all thought and demonstrable, must be entirely a priori. Natural and moral philosophy, on the other hand, can each have an empirical part. Physics has to determine the laws of nature as an object of experience; ethics has to determine the laws of the human will as it is affected by nature. The laws of physics describe how everything actually happens; the laws of ethics describe how everything ought to happen. Ethics must also take account of the conditions under which what ought to happen often does not.

We may call all philosophy empirical so far as it rests on grounds of experience. The philosophy that derives its doctrines from a priori principles alone we may call pure philosophy. When pure philosophy is merely formal, it is logic. When it is restricted to definite objects of the understanding, it is metaphysics.

In this way the idea arises of a twofold metaphysics — a metaphysics of nature and a metaphysics of morals. Physics will therefore have an empirical part and a rational part. The same holds for ethics; but here the empirical part might be given the special name of practical anthropology, while the name morality is reserved for the rational part.

All trades, arts, and crafts have benefited from the division of labour. Instead of one person doing everything, each focuses on a specific kind of work, distinct from the rest in the skills it demands, so that he can do it more easily and to a higher standard. Where the different kinds of work are not separated, where everyone is a jack-of-all-trades, manufacturing remains at the most primitive level. It might be worth asking whether pure philosophy in all its branches doesn't require someone specifically dedicated to it. Would the whole enterprise of science benefit if those who like to mix the rational and empirical together in proportions unknown even to themselves — people who, to please public taste, call themselves independent thinkers and dismiss as nitpickers those who focus only on the rational part — were warned off trying to do two jobs at once that demand very different methods, each perhaps requiring its own special talent, and which combined in one person only produce bunglers? But here I only ask whether the nature of science doesn't require us to keep the empirical and the rational strictly separate, and to prefix to physics proper (or empirical physics) a metaphysics of nature, and to practical anthropology a metaphysics of morals. The metaphysics of morals must be cleared of everything empirical, so that we can see how much pure reason can accomplish in both cases, and from what sources it draws its a priori teaching. This inquiry must be undertaken either by all moralists (whose name is legion) or by some who feel a calling for it.

Since my concern here is moral philosophy, I narrow the question to this: is it not of the utmost importance to construct a pure moral philosophy that is completely cleared of everything empirical and belongs to anthropology? That such a philosophy must be possible is obvious from the common idea of duty and the moral law. Everyone must admit that if a law is to have moral force — that is, to be the basis of an obligation — it must carry absolute necessity with it. The command "Thou shalt not lie," for example, is not valid for human beings alone, as though other rational beings could ignore it. The same goes for all genuine moral laws. The basis of obligation, therefore, must not be sought in the nature of human beings or in the circumstances of the world they find themselves in, but a priori in the conception of pure reason alone. Any other precept founded on principles of mere experience may be universal in certain respects, but to the extent that it rests in the least on empirical grounds — even just for its motive — it can be a practical rule but never a moral law.

So not only are moral laws and their principles essentially distinguished from every other kind of practical knowledge with anything empirical in it; all moral philosophy rests entirely on its pure part. When applied to a human being, it borrows nothing whatever from knowledge of the human being himself (anthropology) but gives a priori laws to him as a rational being. These laws do require a judgement sharpened by experience — first, to know in what cases they apply, and second, to gain access to the human will and effective influence on conduct. Human beings are pulled by so many inclinations that, although capable of the idea of a practical pure reason, they are not so easily able to make it effective in their lives.

A metaphysics of morals is therefore indispensably necessary, not merely for speculative reasons — to investigate the sources of the practical principles found a priori in our reason — but also because morals themselves are liable to all kinds of corruption as long as we lack the guiding thread and supreme standard by which to estimate them correctly. For an action to be morally good, it is not enough that it conforms to the moral law; it must also be done for the sake of the law. Otherwise the conformity is only contingent and uncertain, since a non-moral principle, although it may sometimes produce actions that conform to the law, will also often produce actions that contradict it. Now it is only in a pure philosophy that we can look for the moral law in its purity and authenticity — and in a practical matter this is of the highest importance. We must therefore begin with pure philosophy (metaphysics), and without it there can be no moral philosophy at all. What mixes pure principles with empirical ones doesn't deserve the name of philosophy, for what distinguishes philosophy from common rational knowledge is that philosophy treats in separate sciences what common knowledge grasps only confusedly. Still less does it deserve the name of moral philosophy, since by this confusion it actually spoils the purity of morals themselves and works against its own end.

Let it not be thought that what is demanded here is already present in the propaedeutic that the celebrated Wolf prefixed to his moral philosophy — namely, his so-called general practical philosophy — and that we therefore have no entirely new field to enter. Just because it was meant as a general practical philosophy, it did not consider any particular kind of will — say, one determined solely from a priori principles without any empirical motives, which we might call a pure will. It considered volition in general, with all the actions and conditions that fall under that general heading. This is what distinguishes it from a metaphysics of morals, just as general logic, which treats the acts and rules of thought in general, is distinguished from transcendental philosophy, which treats the particular acts and rules of pure thought — that is, thought whose cognitions are wholly a priori. The metaphysics of morals has to examine the idea and the principles of a possible pure will, not the acts and conditions of human volition generally, which are largely drawn from psychology. It is true that the general moral philosophy talks about moral laws and duty (contrary to all fitness). But this is no objection, for in this respect too those authors stay true to their idea of the subject. They do not distinguish the motives prescribed by reason alone, wholly a priori — which are properly moral — from the empirical motives that the understanding raises to general concepts merely by comparing experiences. Without noticing the difference of their sources and treating them all as homogeneous, they consider only their greater or lesser quantity. This is how they frame their notion of obligation, which, though anything but moral, is all that can be achieved in a philosophy that passes no judgement at all on the origin of all possible practical concepts — whether they are a priori or only a posteriori.

Since I intend to publish a metaphysics of morals later, I am issuing these Fundamental Principles first. There is properly no foundation for a metaphysics of morals other than the critical examination of a pure practical reason — just as the foundation of metaphysics is the critical examination of pure speculative reason, already published. But first, the critical examination of pure practical reason is not so absolutely necessary as that of speculative reason, because in moral matters human reason can easily be brought to a high degree of correctness and completeness, even in the commonest understanding, whereas in its theoretical but pure use it is wholly dialectical. Second, if the critique of a pure practical reason is to be complete, it must also be possible to show its identity with speculative reason in a common principle, since ultimately there can be only one and the same reason, distinguished merely in its application. I could not, however, bring it to that completeness here without introducing considerations of a wholly different kind that would only confuse the reader. For this reason I have called this work Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysics of Morals rather than a Critical Examination of Pure Practical Reason.

Third, since a metaphysics of morals — despite its discouraging title — is capable of being presented in popular form, adapted to ordinary understanding, I find it useful to separate from it this preliminary treatise on its fundamental principles. That way I won't need to drag these unavoidably subtle discussions into a book of a simpler character.

The present treatise is nothing more than the investigation and establishment of the supreme principle of morality. This alone constitutes a study complete in itself, one that should be kept apart from every other moral investigation. My conclusions on this weighty question, which has so far been very unsatisfactorily examined, would no doubt gain considerable support from applying the same principle to the whole system, and would be greatly confirmed by the way it would prove adequate throughout. But I must forgo this advantage, which would after all be more gratifying than useful. The easy applicability of a principle and its apparent adequacy give no really certain proof of its soundness; they tend rather to inspire a partiality that prevents us from examining and estimating it strictly in itself, without regard to consequences.

In this work I have adopted the method I think most suitable, proceeding analytically from common knowledge to the determination of its ultimate principle, and then descending synthetically from the examination of this principle and its sources back to the common knowledge in which we find it employed. The division will therefore be as follows:
1 FIRST SECTION. Transition from the common rational knowledge of morality to the philosophical.
2 SECOND SECTION. Transition from popular moral philosophy to the metaphysics of morals.
3 THIRD SECTION. Final step from the metaphysics of morals to the critique of pure practical reason.
SEC_1
FIRST SECTION
TRANSITION FROM THE COMMON RATIONAL KNOWLEDGE
OF MORALITY TO THE PHILOSOPHICAL

Nothing in the world — or even outside it — can possibly be conceived as good without qualification, except a good will. Intelligence, wit, judgement, and the other talents of the mind, whatever we call them, or courage, resolution, perseverance, as qualities of temperament, are undoubtedly good and desirable in many ways. But these gifts of nature can also become extremely bad and harmful if the will that uses them — the will that constitutes what we call character — is not good. The same goes for the gifts of fortune. Power, wealth, honour, even health, and the general well-being and contentment with one's condition that we call happiness, inspire pride and often presumption, unless there is a good will to correct their influence on the mind and so to rectify the whole principle of acting and adapt it to its end. The sight of a being not adorned with a single trace of a pure and good will, enjoying unbroken prosperity, can never give pleasure to an impartial rational spectator. A good will, then, seems to be the indispensable condition even of being worthy of happiness.

There are some qualities that are useful to this good will itself and may make its work easier, yet have no intrinsic unconditional value, but always presuppose a good will, which limits the esteem we rightly have for them and forbids us to regard them as absolutely good. Moderation in the affections and passions, self-control, and calm deliberation are not only good in many ways but even seem to be part of the intrinsic worth of the person. Yet they are far from deserving to be called good without qualification, although the ancients praised them unconditionally. Without the principles of a good will, they can become extremely bad: the coolness of a villain not only makes him far more dangerous, but also makes him directly more abominable in our eyes than he would have been without it.

A good will is good not because of what it brings about or accomplishes, not because of its fitness for attaining some proposed end, but simply by virtue of the act of willing. That is, it is good in itself, and considered by itself it is to be esteemed far higher than anything that could be produced by it in favour of any inclination — or even the sum total of all inclinations. Even if, by some special misfortune or the stingy provision of a step-motherly nature, this will should completely lack the power to accomplish its purpose; even if with its greatest efforts it should achieve nothing, and there remained only the good will (not, of course, a mere wish, but the summoning of every means in our power) — then, like a jewel, it would still shine by its own light, as something that has its whole value in itself. Its usefulness or fruitlessness can neither add to nor take away from this value. Usefulness would be, as it were, only the setting that lets us handle the jewel more easily in everyday commerce, or that draws the attention of those who are not yet connoisseurs. It cannot recommend the jewel to true connoisseurs or determine its value.

There is, however, something so strange in this idea of the absolute value of the mere will — an idea that takes no account of utility — that, despite the full agreement of even common reason with it, a suspicion must arise that this idea may really be the product of mere high-flown fancy, and that we may have misunderstood nature's purpose in giving reason as the governor of our will. We will therefore examine this idea from that point of view.

In the physical constitution of an organized being — that is, a being adapted suitably to the purposes of life — we take it as a fundamental principle that no organ for any purpose will be found except the one best suited and adapted for that purpose. Now in a being that has reason and a will, if the proper object of nature were its conservation, its welfare — in a word, its happiness — then nature would have made a very bad arrangement in selecting the creature's reason to carry out this purpose. All the actions the creature has to perform with this purpose in view, and the whole rule of its conduct, would have been far more surely prescribed to it by instinct, and that end would have been attained much more reliably than reason could ever achieve. If reason had been given to this favoured creature on top of instinct, it should only have served to contemplate the happy constitution of its nature, to admire it, to congratulate itself on it, and to feel thankful for it to the beneficent cause — not to subject its desires to that weak and delusive guidance and meddle bunglingly with nature's purpose. In a word, nature would have made sure that reason did not break out into practical exercise, nor presume, with its weak insight, to think out for itself the plan of happiness and the means of attaining it. Nature would have taken on herself the choice not only of the ends but also of the means, and with wise foresight would have entrusted both to instinct.

And in fact we find that the more a cultivated reason applies itself with deliberate purpose to the enjoyment of life and happiness, the further the person falls short of true satisfaction. From this circumstance there arises in many — if they are honest enough to admit it — a certain degree of misology, that is, hatred of reason, especially in those most experienced in its use. After calculating all the advantages they derive — I won't say from the invention of all the arts of common luxury, but even from the sciences (which seem to them after all only a luxury of the understanding) — they find they have actually only brought more trouble on their shoulders rather than gained in happiness. They end by envying, rather than despising, the more ordinary type of people who stay closer to the guidance of mere instinct and don't allow reason much influence on their conduct. We must admit that the judgement of those who would very much lower the lofty praise of the advantages reason gives us with regard to the happiness and satisfaction of life, or who would even reduce them below zero, is by no means morose or ungrateful to the goodness with which the world is governed. At the root of those judgements lies the idea that our existence has a different and far nobler end, for which — and not for happiness — reason is properly intended, and which must therefore be regarded as the supreme condition to which the private ends of human beings must, for the most part, be subordinated.

For reason is not competent to guide the will with certainty regarding its objects and the satisfaction of all our needs (which it even multiplies to some extent); an implanted instinct would have led to that end with much greater certainty. Yet reason is nevertheless given to us as a practical faculty — that is, as one meant to have influence on the will. Granting that nature in distributing her capacities has adapted means to ends, the true destination of reason must be to produce a will not merely good as a means to something else, but good in itself. For this, reason was absolutely necessary. This will, although not the sole and complete good, must be the supreme good and the condition of every other, even of the desire for happiness. Under these circumstances, there is nothing inconsistent with the wisdom of nature in the fact that the cultivation of reason, required for the first and unconditional purpose, in many ways interferes — at least in this life — with the attainment of the second, which is always conditional, namely happiness. It may even reduce happiness to nothing, without nature thereby failing of her purpose. For reason recognizes the establishment of a good will as its highest practical destination, and in attaining this purpose is capable only of a satisfaction of its own kind — namely, that which comes from attaining an end determined by reason alone, even though this may involve many disappointments to the ends of inclination.

We now have to develop the notion of a will that deserves to be highly esteemed for itself and is good without a view to anything further — a notion that already exists in sound natural understanding, requiring rather to be clarified than taught, and which in estimating the value of our actions always takes the first place and constitutes the condition of all the rest. To do this, we will take the notion of duty, which includes that of a good will, although under certain subjective restrictions and hindrances. These, however, far from concealing the good will or making it unrecognizable, rather bring it out by contrast and make it shine all the brighter.

I leave aside here all actions already recognized as inconsistent with duty, even if they may be useful for this or that purpose. For with these, the question whether they are done from duty cannot arise at all, since they actually conflict with duty. I also set aside those actions that really do conform to duty, but which people have no direct inclination to perform, doing them only because they are driven to it by some other inclination. For in this case it is easy to tell whether the action that agrees with duty is done from duty or from a selfish motive. It is much harder to make this distinction when the action accords with duty and the subject also has a direct inclination to it. For example, it is always a duty for a shopkeeper not to overcharge an inexperienced customer; and wherever there is much commerce, the prudent merchant does not overcharge but keeps a fixed price for everyone, so that a child can buy from him just as well as anyone else. People are honestly served this way. But this is not enough to make us believe the shopkeeper acted from duty and from principles of honesty: his own advantage required it. It is out of the question in this case to suppose he might in addition have a direct inclination in favour of his customers, so that out of love he gave no one an advantage over another. Accordingly the action was done neither from duty nor from direct inclination, but merely from a selfish motive.

On the other hand, it is a duty to preserve one's life, and in addition everyone has a direct inclination to do so. But on that account the often anxious care most people take for their lives has no intrinsic worth, and their maxim has no moral import. They preserve their life as duty requires, no doubt, but not because duty requires it. On the other hand, if adversity and hopeless sorrow have completely killed the relish for life; if the unfortunate person, strong in mind, indignant at his fate rather than despondent or dejected, wishes for death, and yet preserves his life without loving it — not from inclination or fear, but from duty — then his maxim has a moral worth.

It is a duty to be kind to others when we can. Beyond this, there are many people so sympathetically constituted that, without any motive of vanity or self-interest, they find pleasure in spreading joy around them and can delight in the satisfaction of others when it is their own work. But I maintain that in such a case an action of this kind, however appropriate and amiable it may be, still has no true moral worth. It is on a level with other inclinations — for example, the inclination to honour, which, if it happens to be directed to what is in fact of public utility and consistent with duty and therefore honourable, deserves praise and encouragement, but not esteem. The maxim lacks the moral import — namely, that such actions be done from duty, not from inclination. Suppose the mind of that philanthropist were clouded by his own sorrow, extinguishing all sympathy with the lot of others, and that, while he still has the power to help others in distress, he is not touched by their trouble because he is absorbed with his own. Now suppose he tears himself out of this dead insensibility and performs the action without any inclination to it, but simply from duty — then for the first time his action has its genuine moral worth. Further still: if nature has put little sympathy in the heart of this or that person; if he, an upright man by hypothesis, is by temperament cold and indifferent to the sufferings of others, perhaps because in respect of his own he is provided with the special gift of patience and fortitude, and supposes — or even demands — that others should have the same; and such a person would certainly not be the lowest product of nature — but if nature had not specially fitted him to be a philanthropist, would he not still find in himself a source from which to give himself a far higher worth than that of a good-natured temperament? Unquestionably. It is precisely in this that the moral worth of the character is brought out, which is incomparably the highest of all: that he is kind not from inclination, but from duty.

To secure one's own happiness is a duty, at least indirectly; for discontent with one's condition, under the pressure of many anxieties and amidst unsatisfied wants, might easily become a great temptation to violate duty. But here again, without looking to duty, all human beings already have the strongest and most intimate inclination to happiness, because it is in this very idea that all inclinations are combined into one total. The precept of happiness is, however, often of such a sort that it greatly interferes with some inclinations, and yet a person cannot form any definite and certain conception of the sum of satisfaction of all of them, which is called happiness. It is not surprising, then, that a single inclination, definite as to what it promises and as to the time within which it can be gratified, can often overcome such a fluctuating idea. A gouty patient, for instance, can choose to enjoy what he likes and to suffer what he may, since on his calculation he has at least on this occasion not sacrificed the enjoyment of the present moment to a possibly mistaken expectation of a happiness that is supposed to lie in health. But even in this case, if the general desire for happiness did not influence his will, and supposing that in his particular case health was not a necessary element in this calculation, there yet remains in this case — as in all others — this law: that he should promote his happiness not from inclination but from duty. By this his conduct would first acquire true moral worth.

It is undoubtedly in this manner that we are to understand those passages of Scripture in which we are commanded to love our neighbour, even our enemy. For love, as an affection, cannot be commanded; but kindness for duty's sake can be — even when we are not impelled to it by any inclination, indeed are repelled by a natural and unconquerable aversion. This is practical love, not pathological love — a love seated in the will and not in the propensities of sense, in principles of action and not of tender sympathy. And it is this love alone which can be commanded.

The second proposition is: an action done from duty derives its moral worth not from the purpose to be attained by it, but from the maxim by which it is determined. It therefore does not depend on the realization of the object of the action, but only on the principle of volition by which the action takes place, regardless of any object of desire. It is clear from what precedes that the purposes we may have in view in our actions, or their effects regarded as ends and springs of the will, cannot give actions any unconditional or moral worth. In what, then, can their worth lie, if it is not to consist in the will in relation to its expected effect? It cannot lie anywhere but in the principle of the will, regardless of the ends that can be attained by the action. For the will stands, as it were, between its a priori principle, which is formal, and its a posteriori spring, which is material — as between two roads. It must be determined by something; so when an action is done from duty, it must be determined by the formal principle of volition, every material principle having been withdrawn from it.

The third proposition, which is a consequence of the two preceding ones, I would express like this: duty is the necessity of acting from respect for the law. I may have inclination for an object as the effect of my proposed action, but I cannot have respect for it, just because it is an effect and not an energy of will. Similarly I cannot have respect for inclination, whether my own or someone else's. At most, if it is my own, I can approve of it; if it is another's, I can sometimes even love it — that is, look on it as favourable to my own interest. Only what is connected with my will as a principle, in no way as an effect — what does not subserve my inclination but overpowers it, or at least excludes it from the calculation in the case of choice — in other words, simply the law itself, can be an object of respect, and so a command. Now an action done from duty must wholly exclude the influence of inclination and with it every object of the will, so that nothing remains that can determine the will except, objectively, the law, and subjectively, pure respect for this practical law. The maxim* that follows is that I should follow this law even at the cost of thwarting all my inclinations.

* A maxim is the subjective principle of volition. The objective principle (the one that would also serve subjectively as a practical principle for all rational beings if reason had full power over the faculty of desire) is the practical law.

Thus the moral worth of an action does not lie in the effect expected from it, nor in any principle of action that has to borrow its motive from this expected effect. For all these effects — agreeableness of one's condition and even the promotion of the happiness of others — could have been brought about by other causes too, so that the will of a rational being would not be needed for them. Yet it is in the will alone that the supreme and unconditional good can be found. The pre-eminent good we call moral can therefore consist in nothing but the conception of law in itself, which is of course only possible in a rational being, insofar as this conception, and not the expected effect, determines the will. This is a good already present in the person who acts accordingly, and we do not have to wait for it to appear first in the result. *

* It might be objected here that I take refuge behind the word "respect" in an obscure feeling, instead of giving a distinct solution of the question by a concept of reason. But although respect is a feeling, it is not a feeling received through influence; it is self-produced by a rational concept, and is therefore specifically distinct from all feelings of the former kind, which may be referred to either inclination or fear. What I recognize immediately as a law for me, I recognize with respect. This merely signifies the consciousness that my will is subordinate to a law, without the intervention of other influences on my sense. The immediate determination of the will by the law, and the consciousness of this, is called respect, so that it is regarded as an effect of the law on the subject, not as its cause. Respect is properly the conception of a worth that thwarts my self-love. Accordingly it is something considered neither as an object of inclination nor of fear, although it has something analogous to both. The object of respect is the law alone — the law we impose on ourselves and yet recognize as necessary in itself. As a law, we are subjected to it without consulting self-love; as imposed by us on ourselves, it is a result of our will. In the former aspect it has an analogy to fear, in the latter to inclination. Respect for a person is properly only respect for the law (of honesty, etc.) of which he gives us an example. Since we also regard the improvement of our talents as a duty, we consider that we see in a person of talent, as it were, the example of a law (namely, to become like him in this by practice), and this constitutes our respect. All so-called moral interest consists simply in respect for the law.

But what sort of law can that be, the conception of which must determine the will, even without paying any regard to the effect expected from it, in order that this will may be called good absolutely and without qualification? Since I have deprived the will of every impulse that could arise from obedience to any particular law, there remains nothing but the universal conformity of its actions to law in general, which alone is to serve the will as a principle. That is: I am never to act otherwise than so that I could also will that my maxim should become a universal law. Here it is the simple conformity to law in general — without assuming any particular law applicable to certain actions — that serves the will as its principle, and must serve it so, if duty is not to be an empty delusion and a chimerical notion. The common reason of human beings in its practical judgements coincides perfectly with this and always has in view the principle here suggested. Take for example this question: may I, when in distress, make a promise with the intention of not keeping it? I readily distinguish two senses the question may have: is it prudent, or is it right, to make a false promise? The first may undoubtedly often be the case. I see clearly that it is not enough to extricate myself from a present difficulty by means of this subterfuge; I have to weigh whether much greater inconvenience may not in future spring from this lie than from the trouble I now escape. With all my supposed cunning, the consequences cannot be foreseen so easily but that credit once lost may be far more damaging to me than any mischief I now try to avoid. So I should consider whether it would not be more prudent to act on a universal maxim and make it a habit to promise nothing except with the intention of keeping it. But it soon becomes clear that such a maxim would still rest only on the fear of consequences. Now it is wholly different to be truthful from duty and to be truthful from fear of bad consequences. In the first case, the very notion of the action already implies a law for me; in the second, I must first look around for the results that might affect me. For to deviate from the principle of duty is beyond doubt wicked; but to be unfaithful to my maxim of prudence may often be very advantageous to me, although sticking to it is certainly safer. The shortest, and an unerring, way to discover the answer to the question whether a lying promise is consistent with duty is to ask myself: "Would I be content that my maxim (to extricate myself from difficulty by a false promise) should hold good as a universal law, for myself as well as for others?" Could I say to myself: "Anyone may make a deceitful promise when he finds himself in a difficulty he cannot otherwise escape"? I quickly become aware that while I can will the lie, I cannot by any means will that lying should be a universal law. For with such a law there would be no promises at all, since it would be useless to declare my intention regarding future actions to people who would not believe my declaration, or who, if they hastily did believe it, would pay me back in my own coin. Hence my maxim, as soon as it should be made a universal law, would necessarily destroy itself.

I therefore do not need any far-reaching penetration to discern what I have to do in order that my will may be morally good. Inexperienced in the course of the world, incapable of being prepared for all its contingencies, I only ask myself: can you also will that your maxim should be a universal law? If not, then it must be rejected — not because of any disadvantage it might bring me or even others, but because it cannot enter as a principle into a possible universal legislation, and reason extorts from me immediate respect for such legislation. I do not yet discern on what this respect is based (the philosopher may inquire into that), but at least I understand that it is an estimation of the worth that far outweighs all the worth of what is recommended by inclination, and that the necessity of acting from pure respect for the practical law is what constitutes duty, to which every other motive must give way, because it is the condition of a will being good in itself, and the worth of such a will is above everything.

Thus, without leaving the moral knowledge of common human reason, we have arrived at its principle. Ordinary people do not, of course, conceive it in such an abstract and universal form, but they always have it really before their eyes and use it as the standard of their decisions. It would be easy to show how, with this compass in hand, people are well able to distinguish in every case what is good or bad, consistent with duty or not — if, without teaching them anything new, we only, like Socrates, direct their attention to the principle they themselves employ. So we don't need science and philosophy to know what to do in order to be honest and good, or even wise and virtuous. We might have guessed in advance that the knowledge of what every person is bound to do, and therefore also to know, would be within reach of every person, even the most ordinary. We cannot help admiring the great advantage that the practical judgement has over the theoretical in common human understanding. In the theoretical sphere, if common reason ventures to depart from the laws of experience and the perceptions of the senses, it falls into mere inconceivabilities and self-contradictions, or at least into a chaos of uncertainty, obscurity, and instability. But in the practical sphere, it is precisely when common understanding excludes all sensible springs from practical laws that its power of judgement begins to show to advantage. It then even becomes subtle, whether it is splitting hairs with its own conscience or with other claims about what should be called right, or whether it wants to determine honestly, for its own instruction, the worth of actions. In the latter case it may have as good a hope of hitting the mark as any philosopher whatever. Indeed it is almost more sure of doing so, because the philosopher can have no other principle, yet may easily confuse his judgement by a multitude of considerations foreign to the matter, and so turn aside from the right way. Would it not therefore be wiser in moral matters to acquiesce in the judgement of common reason, or at most to call in philosophy only to make the system of morals more complete and intelligible and its rules more convenient for use (especially for disputation) — but not to draw the common understanding away from its happy simplicity, or lead it by means of philosophy into a new path of inquiry and instruction?

Innocence is indeed a glorious thing, but on the other hand it is very sad that it cannot well maintain itself and is easily seduced. On that account even wisdom — which otherwise consists more in conduct than in knowledge — needs science, not in order to learn from it, but to secure for its precepts admission and permanence. Against all the commands of duty that reason presents to a person as so worthy of respect, he feels in himself a powerful counterweight in his wants and inclinations, the complete satisfaction of which he sums up under the name of happiness. Reason issues its commands unyieldingly, without promising anything to the inclinations, and as it were with disregard and contempt for their claims, which are so impetuous and at the same time so plausible, and which will not allow themselves to be suppressed by any command. Hence there arises a natural dialectic — that is, a disposition to argue against these strict laws of duty and to question their validity, or at least their purity and strictness; and, if possible, to bring them more into line with our wishes and inclinations — in other words, to corrupt them at their very source and entirely destroy their worth, a thing that even common practical reason cannot ultimately call good.

In this way the common reason of human beings is compelled to step outside its sphere and take a step into the field of a practical philosophy — not to satisfy any speculative need (which never occurs to it so long as it is content to be mere sound reason), but on practical grounds, to obtain information and clear instruction about the source of its principle and the correct determination of it against the maxims based on wants and inclinations. This way it can escape from the perplexity of opposing claims and not run the risk of losing all genuine moral principles through the ambiguity into which it easily falls. So when practical reason cultivates itself, there imperceptibly arises in it a dialectic that forces it to seek help in philosophy, just as happens to it in its theoretical use; and in this case, as in the other, it will find rest nowhere except in a thorough critical examination of our reason.
SEC_2
SECOND SECTION
TRANSITION FROM POPULAR MORAL PHILOSOPHY
TO THE METAPHYSICS OF MORALS

If until now we have drawn our notion of duty from the common use of our practical reason, this does not in the least mean we have treated it as an empirical notion. On the contrary, if we attend to people's actual conduct, we meet frequent and (as we ourselves grant) just complaints that no certain example of the disposition to act from pure duty can be found. Although many things are done in conformity with what duty prescribes, it is nevertheless always doubtful whether they are done strictly from duty and so have moral worth. For this reason, there have always been philosophers who have flatly denied that this disposition exists at all in human actions, and have ascribed everything to a more or less refined self-love. They did not therefore question the soundness of the concept of morality. On the contrary, they spoke with sincere regret of the frailty and corruption of human nature, which, though noble enough to take as its rule an idea so worthy of respect, is yet too weak to follow it, and uses the reason that ought to give it the law only for providing for the interests of the inclinations — whether individually, or at best in the greatest possible harmony with one another.

In fact, it is absolutely impossible to establish by experience with complete certainty a single case in which the maxim of an action, however right in itself, rested simply on moral grounds and on the concept of duty. Sometimes it happens that with the sharpest self-examination we can find nothing besides the moral principle of duty that could have been powerful enough to move us to this or that action and to so great a sacrifice. But we cannot from this infer with certainty that it was not really some secret impulse of self-love, under the false appearance of duty, that was the actual determining cause of the will. We like to flatter ourselves by falsely claiming a more noble motive; yet in fact we can never, even by the strictest examination, get completely behind the secret springs of action. For when the question concerns moral worth, what matters is not the actions we see but their inward principles, which we do not see.

What is more, we cannot better serve the wishes of those who ridicule all morality as a mere chimera of human imagination overstepping itself out of vanity, than by granting them that notions of duty must be drawn only from experience (as people, out of indolence, are ready to think is also the case with all other notions). This is to prepare a certain triumph for them. Out of love of humanity I am willing to admit that even most of our actions are correct. But if we look closer, we everywhere come upon the dear self that is always conspicuous, and it is this that they have in view — not the strict command of duty, which would often require self-denial. Without being an enemy of virtue, a cool observer, one who does not mistake the wish for the good, however lively, for its reality, may sometimes doubt whether true virtue is actually found anywhere in the world. This especially as the years go on and judgement is partly made wiser by experience and partly more acute in observation. This being so, nothing can secure us from falling away entirely from our ideas of duty, or maintain in the soul a well-grounded respect for its law, except the clear conviction that even if there should never have been actions that really sprang from such pure sources, the question is not whether this or that takes place; rather, that reason of itself, independent of all experience, ordains what ought to take place. Accordingly, actions of which the world has perhaps so far given no example, the feasibility of which might even be very much doubted by someone who founds everything on experience, are nevertheless inflexibly commanded by reason. For instance, even though there may never yet have been a sincere friend, none the less is pure sincerity in friendship required of every person, because prior to all experience this duty is involved as duty in the idea of a reason determining the will by a priori principles.

When we add further that, unless we deny that the notion of morality has any truth or reference to any possible object, we must admit that its law must be valid not merely for human beings but for all rational creatures in general — not merely under certain contingent conditions or with exceptions, but with absolute necessity — then it is clear that no experience could enable us to infer even the possibility of such apodeictic laws. For with what right could we bring into unbounded respect, as a universal precept for every rational nature, something that perhaps holds only under the contingent conditions of humanity? Or how could laws of the determination of our will be regarded as laws of the determination of the will of rational beings in general, and for us only as such, if they were merely empirical and did not take their origin wholly a priori from pure but practical reason?

Nor could anything be more fatal to morality than that we should wish to derive it from examples. For every example of it that is set before me must first itself be tested by principles of morality, to see whether it is worthy to serve as an original example — that is, as a pattern. By no means can an example authoritatively furnish the conception of morality. Even the Holy One of the Gospels must first be compared with our ideal of moral perfection before we can recognize him as such; and so he says of himself, "Why call me (whom you see) good? None is good (the model of good) but God only (whom you do not see)." But from where do we get the conception of God as the supreme good? Simply from the idea of moral perfection, which reason frames a priori and connects inseparably with the notion of a free will. Imitation has no place at all in morality, and examples serve only for encouragement — that is, they put beyond doubt the feasibility of what the law commands; they make visible what the practical rule expresses more generally. But they can never authorize us to set aside the true original, which lies in reason, and to guide ourselves by examples.

If, then, there is no genuine supreme principle of morality except one that must rest simply on pure reason, independent of all experience, I think it is not even necessary to ask whether it is good to exhibit these concepts in their generality (in abstracto) as they are established a priori, along with the principles belonging to them — if our knowledge is to be distinguished from common knowledge and called philosophical.

In our times this might perhaps be necessary; for if we took a vote on whether pure rational knowledge separated from everything empirical (that is, the metaphysics of morals) or popular practical philosophy is to be preferred, it is easy to guess which side would win.

Descending to popular notions is certainly very commendable, if the ascent to the principles of pure reason has first taken place and been satisfactorily accomplished. This means that we first found ethics on metaphysics, and then, once it is firmly established, secure a hearing for it by giving it a popular character. But it is quite absurd to try to be popular in the first inquiry, on which the soundness of the principles depends. Not only can this procedure never lay claim to the very rare merit of a true philosophical popularity — there is no art in being intelligible if one renounces all thoroughness of insight — but it also produces a disgusting medley of compiled observations and half-reasoned principles. Shallow heads enjoy this because it can be used for everyday chat. But the shrewd find in it only confusion, and being unsatisfied and unable to help themselves, they look away. Philosophers, who see right through this delusion, get little hearing when they call people off for a time from this pretended popularity, in order that they might be rightly popular only after gaining definite insight.

We need only look at the attempts of moralists in that favourite fashion, and we find at one moment the special constitution of human nature (which also includes, however, the idea of a rational nature in general), at another moment perfection, at another happiness, here moral sense, there fear of God — a little of this and a little of that, in marvellous mixture — without its occurring to them to ask whether the principles of morality are to be sought in the knowledge of human nature at all (which we can have only from experience). If they are not — if these principles are to be found entirely a priori, free from everything empirical, in pure rational concepts only and nowhere else, not even in the smallest degree — then it would be better to adopt the method of making this a separate inquiry, as pure practical philosophy or (if one may use a name so decried) as a metaphysics of morals, * to bring it by itself to completeness, and to require the public, which wants popular treatment, to await the result of this undertaking.

* Just as pure mathematics is distinguished from applied, and pure logic from applied, so if we choose we may also distinguish the pure philosophy of morals (metaphysics) from applied (that is, applied to human nature). This designation also reminds us at once that moral principles are not based on properties of human nature, but must subsist a priori of themselves, while from such principles practical rules must be capable of being deduced for every rational nature, and accordingly for that of human beings as well.

Such a metaphysics of morals, completely isolated, not mixed with any anthropology, theology, physics, or hyperphysics — and still less with occult qualities (which we might call hypophysical) — is not only an indispensable substratum of all sound theoretical knowledge of duties; it is at the same time a desideratum of the highest importance to the actual fulfilment of their precepts. For the pure conception of duty, unmixed with any foreign addition of empirical attractions — in a word, the conception of the moral law — exercises on the human heart, by way of reason alone (which first becomes aware here that it can of itself be practical), an influence so much more powerful than all other springs * that may be derived from the field of experience, that in the consciousness of its worth it despises the latter and can by degrees become their master. Whereas a mixed ethics, compounded partly of motives drawn from feelings and inclinations and partly of conceptions of reason, must make the mind waver between motives that cannot be brought under any principle, that lead to good only by mere accident, and very often also to evil.

* I have a letter from the late excellent Sulzer in which he asks me what could be the reason that moral instruction, although containing much that is convincing for reason, accomplishes so little. My answer was postponed in order that I might make it complete. But it is simply this: the teachers themselves have not got their own notions clear, and when they try to make up for this by raking up motives of moral goodness from every quarter, trying to make their medicine right strong, they spoil it. For the commonest understanding shows that if we imagine on the one hand an act of honesty done with steadfast mind, apart from every view to advantage of any kind in this world or another, and even under the greatest temptations of necessity or allurement, and on the other hand a similar act that was affected, however slightly, by a foreign motive, the former leaves the second far behind and eclipses it. It elevates the soul and inspires the wish to be able to act in like manner oneself. Even moderately young children feel this impression, and one should never represent duties to them in any other light.

From what has been said, it is clear that all moral conceptions have their seat and origin completely a priori in reason — and this in the commonest reason just as truly as in the most highly speculative; that they cannot be obtained by abstraction from any empirical, and therefore merely contingent, knowledge; that it is precisely this purity of their origin that makes them worthy to serve as our supreme practical principle; and that just in proportion as we add anything empirical, we detract from their genuine influence and from the absolute value of actions. It is not only of the greatest necessity from a purely speculative point of view, but also of the greatest practical importance, to derive these notions and laws from pure reason, to present them pure and unmixed, and even to determine the scope of this practical or pure rational knowledge — that is, to determine the whole faculty of pure practical reason. In doing so, we must not make its principles dependent on the particular nature of human reason (though in speculative philosophy this may be permitted, or may even at times be necessary). Since moral laws ought to hold good for every rational creature, we must derive them from the general concept of a rational being. In this way, although for its application to human beings morality has need of anthropology, we must in the first instance treat it independently as pure philosophy — that is, as metaphysics, complete in itself (a thing easily done in such distinct branches of science) — knowing well that unless we are in possession of this, it would not only be vain to determine the moral element of duty in right actions for purposes of speculative criticism; it would be impossible to base morals on their genuine principles even for common practical purposes, especially of moral instruction, so as to produce pure moral dispositions and engraft them on people's minds for the promotion of the greatest possible good in the world.

But to make sure that in this study we do not merely advance by the natural steps from the common moral judgement (in this case very worthy of respect) to the philosophical, as has already been done, but also from a popular philosophy that goes no further than it can reach by groping with the help of examples, to metaphysics (which does not allow itself to be checked by anything empirical and, as it must measure the whole extent of this kind of rational knowledge, goes as far as ideal conceptions, where even examples fail us), we must follow and clearly describe the practical faculty of reason, from the general rules of its determination to the point where the notion of duty springs from it.

Everything in nature works according to laws. Rational beings alone have the faculty of acting according to the conception of laws — that is, according to principles — in other words, they have a will. Since the deduction of actions from principles requires reason, the will is nothing other than practical reason. If reason infallibly determines the will, then the actions of such a being that are recognized as objectively necessary are subjectively necessary too — that is, the will is a faculty to choose only what reason, independent of inclination, recognizes as practically necessary, that is, as good. But if reason by itself does not sufficiently determine the will; if the will is also subject to subjective conditions (particular impulses) that do not always coincide with the objective ones; in a word, if the will does not in itself completely accord with reason (which is actually the case with human beings) — then the actions that objectively are recognized as necessary are subjectively contingent, and the determination of such a will according to objective laws is obligation. That is to say, the relation of the objective laws to a will that is not thoroughly good is conceived as the determination of the will of a rational being by principles of reason, principles that the will, from its nature, does not necessarily follow.
The conception of an objective principle, so far as it is obligatory for a will, is called a command (of reason), and the formula of the command is called an imperative.

All imperatives are expressed by the word "ought" (or "shall"), and so indicate the relation of an objective law of reason to a will that, by its subjective constitution, is not necessarily determined by it (an obligation). Imperatives say that something would be good to do or to refrain from, but they say it to a will that does not always do a thing just because it is conceived as good to do. What is practically good, however, is what determines the will by means of conceptions of reason — and consequently not from subjective causes but objectively, on principles valid for every rational being as such. This is distinguished from the pleasant, which influences the will only by means of sensation from merely subjective causes, valid only for the senses of this or that individual, and not as a principle of reason that holds for everyone. *

* The dependence of the desires on sensations is called inclination, and this accordingly always indicates a want. The dependence of a contingently determinable will on principles of reason is called an interest. This is found only in the case of a dependent will, one that does not always of itself conform to reason; in the Divine will we cannot conceive any interest. But the human will can also take an interest in a thing without therefore acting from interest. The former signifies the practical interest in the action, the latter the pathological interest in the object of the action. The former indicates only dependence of the will on principles of reason in themselves; the second, dependence on principles of reason for the sake of inclination, reason supplying only the practical rules for how the requirement of inclination may be satisfied. In the first case the action interests me; in the second the object of the action (because it is pleasant to me). We have seen in the first section that in an action done from duty we must look not to the interest in the object, but only to the interest in the action itself, and in its rational principle (namely, the law).

A perfectly good will would therefore be equally subject to objective laws (laws of the good), but could not be conceived as obliged thereby to act lawfully, because of itself, from its subjective constitution, it can only be determined by the conception of the good. Therefore no imperatives hold for the Divine will, or in general for a holy will. "Ought" is here out of place, because the volition is already of itself necessarily in unison with the law. Imperatives are therefore only formulae to express the relation of objective laws of all volition to the subjective imperfection of the will of this or that rational being — for example, the human will.

Now all imperatives command either hypothetically or categorically. The former represent the practical necessity of a possible action as a means to something else that is willed (or that one might possibly will). The categorical imperative would be one that represented an action as necessary of itself, without reference to another end — that is, as objectively necessary.

Since every practical law represents a possible action as good, and on this account as necessary for a subject who is practically determinable by reason, all imperatives are formulae determining an action that is necessary according to the principle of a will good in some respect. If the action is good only as a means to something else, the imperative is hypothetical; if it is conceived as good in itself, and consequently as necessarily the principle of a will that of itself conforms to reason, then it is categorical.

Thus the imperative declares what action possible by me would be good and presents the practical rule in relation to a will that does not immediately perform an action just because it is good — whether because the subject does not always know that it is good, or because, even knowing this, its maxims might be opposed to the objective principles of practical reason.

Accordingly the hypothetical imperative only says that the action is good for some purpose, possible or actual. In the first case it is a problematical, in the second an assertorial practical principle. The categorical imperative, which declares an action to be objectively necessary in itself, without reference to any purpose — that is, without any other end — is valid as an apodeictic (practical) principle.

Whatever is possible only by the power of some rational being may also be conceived as a possible purpose of some will. The principles of action with regard to the means necessary to attain some possible purpose are therefore in fact infinitely numerous. All sciences have a practical part, consisting of problems expressing that some end is possible for us, and of imperatives directing how it may be attained. These may therefore be called in general imperatives of skill. Here there is no question whether the end is rational and good, but only what one must do in order to attain it. The precepts for the physician to make his patient thoroughly healthy, and for a poisoner to ensure certain death, are of equal value in this respect, that each serves to effect its purpose perfectly. Since in early youth we cannot know what ends are likely to occur to us in the course of life, parents seek to have their children taught a great many things, and provide for their skill in the use of means for all sorts of arbitrary ends, of none of which can they determine whether it may not perhaps in future be an object to their pupil, but which it is at any rate possible that he might aim at. This anxiety is so great that they commonly neglect to form and correct their children's judgement on the value of the things that may be chosen as ends.

There is one end, however, that may be assumed to be actually such to all rational beings (so far as imperatives apply to them, namely as dependent beings), and therefore one purpose that they not merely may have, but that we may with certainty assume they all actually have by a natural necessity — and this is happiness. The hypothetical imperative which expresses the practical necessity of an action as means to the advancement of happiness is assertorial. We are not to present it as necessary for an uncertain and merely possible purpose, but for a purpose that we may presuppose with certainty and a priori in every person, because it belongs to his being. Now skill in the choice of means to one's own greatest well-being may be called prudence, * in the narrowest sense. And so the imperative that refers to the choice of means to one's own happiness — that is, the precept of prudence — is still always hypothetical. The action is not commanded absolutely, but only as a means to another purpose.

* The word "prudence" is taken in two senses: in one it may bear the name of knowledge of the world, in the other that of private prudence. The former is a person's ability to influence others so as to use them for his own purposes. The latter is the sagacity to combine all these purposes for his own lasting benefit. The latter is properly that to which the value even of the former is reduced; and when someone is prudent in the former sense but not in the latter, we might better say of him that he is clever and cunning, but on the whole imprudent.

Finally, there is an imperative that commands a certain conduct immediately, without having as its condition any other purpose to be attained by it. This imperative is categorical. It concerns not the matter of the action, or its intended result, but its form and the principle of which it is itself a result; and what is essentially good in it consists in the mental disposition, let the consequence be what it may. This imperative may be called the imperative of morality.

There is also a marked distinction between the volitions on these three sorts of principles, in the dissimilarity of the obligation of the will. To mark this difference more clearly, I think they would be most suitably named in their order if we said they are either rules of skill, or counsels of prudence, or commands (laws) of morality. For only law involves the conception of an unconditional and objective necessity, which is consequently universally valid; and commands are laws that must be obeyed — that is, followed even in opposition to inclination. Counsels do indeed involve necessity, but a necessity that can only hold under a contingent subjective condition: they depend on whether this or that person counts this or that as part of his happiness. The categorical imperative, on the contrary, is not limited by any condition, and as being absolutely (though practically) necessary, may quite properly be called a command. We might also call the first kind of imperatives technical (belonging to art), the second pragmatic * (belonging to welfare), the third moral (belonging to free conduct in general, that is, to morals).

* It seems to me that the proper meaning of the word "pragmatic" can be most accurately defined this way. Sanctions are called pragmatic that flow properly not from the law of states as necessary enactments, but from precaution for the general welfare. A history is composed pragmatically when it teaches prudence — that is, instructs the world how it can provide for its interests better than, or at least as well as, the people of former times did.

The question now arises: how are all these imperatives possible? This question does not ask how we can conceive the accomplishment of the action that the imperative commands, but only how we can conceive the obligation of the will that the imperative expresses. No special explanation is needed to show how an imperative of skill is possible. Whoever wills the end, wills also (so far as reason decides his conduct) the means in his power that are indispensably necessary to it. This proposition is, as regards the volition, analytical; for in willing an object as my effect, the causality of myself as an acting cause — that is, the use of the means — is already thought; and the imperative draws from the conception of willing an end the conception of the actions necessary to that end. Synthetical propositions must no doubt be employed in defining the means to a proposed end, but they do not concern the principle, the act of the will, but only the object and its realization. For example, the proposition that, in order to bisect a line on an unerring principle I must draw from its endpoints two intersecting arcs — this is taught only by mathematics in synthetical propositions. But if I know that the intended operation can be performed only by this process, then to say that, if I fully will the operation, I also will the action required for it, is an analytical proposition. For it is one and the same thing to conceive something as an effect that I can produce in a certain way, and to conceive myself as acting in this way.

If it were only equally easy to give a definite conception of happiness, the imperatives of prudence would correspond exactly with those of skill, and would likewise be analytical. For in this case as in that, it could be said: "Whoever wills the end, wills also (according to the dictate of reason necessarily) the indispensable means to it that are in his power." But unfortunately the notion of happiness is so indefinite that although every person wishes to attain it, no one can ever say definitely and consistently what it is that he really wishes and wills. The reason is that all the elements that belong to the notion of happiness are wholly empirical — they must be borrowed from experience — and yet the idea of happiness requires an absolute whole, a maximum of welfare in my present and all future circumstances. Now it is impossible that the most clear-sighted and at the same time most powerful being (supposed finite) should frame for himself a definite conception of what he really wills in this. Does he will riches? How much anxiety, envy, and snares might he not draw on his shoulders by them. Does he will knowledge and discernment? Perhaps it might prove to be only a sharper eye showing him so much the more fearfully the evils that are now concealed from him and cannot be avoided, or imposing more wants on his desires, which already give him enough concern. Would he have a long life? Who guarantees that it would not be a long misery? Would he at least have health? How often has uneasiness of the body restrained someone from excesses into which perfect health would have allowed him to fall? And so on. In short, he is unable on any principle to determine with certainty what would make him truly happy, because to do so he would need to be omniscient. We cannot therefore act on any definite principles to secure happiness, but only on empirical counsels — for example, of diet, frugality, courtesy, reserve, and so on — which experience teaches do, on the average, most promote well-being. From this it follows that the imperatives of prudence do not, strictly speaking, command at all. They cannot present actions objectively as practically necessary; they are rather to be regarded as counsels (consilia) than as precepts of reason. The problem of determining certainly and universally what action would promote the happiness of a rational being is completely insoluble, and consequently no imperative respecting it is possible that should, in the strict sense, command us to do what makes happy. Happiness is not an ideal of reason but of imagination, resting solely on empirical grounds; and it is vain to expect that these should define an action by which one could attain the totality of a series of consequences that is really endless. This imperative of prudence would, however, be an analytical proposition if we assumed that the means to happiness could be certainly assigned; for it is distinguished from the imperative of skill only by this, that in the latter the end is merely possible, while in the former it is given. As both only ordain the means to what we suppose to be willed as an end, it follows that the imperative which ordains the willing of the means to him who wills the end is in both cases analytical. So there is no difficulty regarding the possibility of an imperative of this kind either.

On the other hand, the question how the imperative of morality is possible is undoubtedly the one — the only one — demanding a solution. For this imperative is not at all hypothetical, and the objective necessity it presents cannot rest on any hypothesis, as is the case with the hypothetical imperatives. Only here we must never leave out of consideration that we cannot make out by any example — in other words, empirically — whether there is such an imperative at all; rather we have to fear that all those that seem to be categorical may yet at bottom be hypothetical. For instance, when the precept is "You shall not promise deceitfully," and it is assumed that the necessity of this is not a mere counsel to avoid some other evil — so that it should mean: "You shall not make a lying promise lest, if it become known, you should destroy your credit" — but rather that an action of this kind must be regarded as evil in itself, so that the imperative of the prohibition is categorical, then we cannot show with certainty in any example that the will was determined merely by the law, without any other spring of action, although it may appear to be so. For it is always possible that fear of disgrace, or perhaps an obscure dread of other dangers, may have had a secret influence on the will. Who can prove by experience the non-existence of a cause when all experience tells us is that we do not perceive it? But in such a case the so-called moral imperative, which as such appears to be categorical and unconditional, would in reality only be a pragmatic precept, drawing our attention to our own interests and merely teaching us to take these into consideration.

We shall therefore have to investigate a priori the possibility of a categorical imperative, since in this case we do not have the advantage of its reality being given in experience, so that the elucidation of its possibility should be required only for its explanation, not for its establishment. In the meantime it may be discerned in advance that the categorical imperative alone has the import of a practical law; all the rest may indeed be called principles of the will but not laws, since whatever is only necessary for the attainment of some arbitrary purpose may be considered as in itself contingent, and we can at any time be free from the precept if we give up the purpose. On the contrary, the unconditional command leaves the will no liberty to choose the opposite; it alone therefore carries with it that necessity which we require in a law.

Secondly, in the case of this categorical imperative or law of morality, the difficulty of discerning its possibility is a very profound one. It is an a priori synthetical practical proposition; * and since there is so much difficulty in discerning the possibility of speculative propositions of this kind, it may readily be supposed that the difficulty will be no less with the practical.

* I connect the act with the will without presupposing any condition resulting from any inclination, but a priori, and therefore necessarily (though only objectively, that is, assuming the idea of a reason possessing full power over all subjective motives). This is accordingly a practical proposition that does not deduce the willing of an action by mere analysis from another already presupposed (for we have no such perfect will), but connects it immediately with the conception of the will of a rational being, as something not contained in that conception.

In this problem we will first inquire whether the mere conception of a categorical imperative may not perhaps also supply us with the formula of it — containing the proposition that alone can be a categorical imperative. For even if we know the tenor of such an absolute command, how it is possible will require further special and laborious study, which we postpone to the last section.

When I conceive a hypothetical imperative, I do not in general know beforehand what it will contain until I am given the condition. But when I conceive a categorical imperative, I know at once what it contains. For since the imperative contains, besides the law, only the necessity that the maxims * shall conform to this law, while the law contains no conditions restricting it, there remains nothing but the general statement that the maxim of the action should conform to a universal law; and it is this conformity alone that the imperative properly represents as necessary.

* A maxim is a subjective principle of action, and must be distinguished from the objective principle — namely, practical law. The former contains the practical rule set by reason according to the conditions of the subject (often his ignorance or his inclinations), so that it is the principle on which the subject acts. The law, on the other hand, is the objective principle, valid for every rational being, and the principle on which it ought to act — that is, an imperative.
There is therefore only one categorical imperative, namely this: Act only on that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.

Now if all imperatives of duty can be deduced from this one imperative as from their principle, then, although it should remain undecided whether what is called duty is not merely a vain notion, we shall at least be able to show what we understand by it and what this notion means.

Since the universality of the law according to which effects are produced constitutes what is properly called nature in the most general sense (as to its form) — that is, the existence of things so far as it is determined by general laws — the imperative of duty may be expressed like this: Act as if the maxim of your action were to become by your will a universal law of nature.
We will now enumerate a few duties, adopting the usual division of them into duties to ourselves and to others, and into perfect and imperfect duties. *

* It must be noted here that I reserve the division of duties for a future metaphysics of morals, so that I give it here only as an arbitrary one (in order to arrange my examples). For the rest, I understand by a perfect duty one that admits of no exception in favour of inclination, and then I have not merely external but also internal perfect duties. This is contrary to the use of the word adopted in the schools, but I do not intend to justify it here, since for my purpose it is all one whether it is admitted or not.

1. A man reduced to despair by a series of misfortunes feels weary of life, but is still so far in possession of his reason that he can ask himself whether it would not be contrary to his duty to himself to take his own life. Now he asks whether the maxim of his action could become a universal law of nature. His maxim is: "From self-love, I adopt it as a principle to shorten my life when its longer duration is likely to bring more evil than satisfaction." The question, then, is simply whether this principle, founded on self-love, can become a universal law of nature. Now we see at once that a system of nature in which it should be a law to destroy life by means of the very feeling whose special nature it is to impel to the improvement of life would contradict itself, and therefore could not exist as a system of nature. Hence that maxim cannot possibly hold as a universal law of nature, and is consequently wholly inconsistent with the supreme principle of all duty.

2. Another man finds himself forced by necessity to borrow money. He knows he will not be able to repay it, but sees also that nothing will be lent to him unless he firmly promises to repay it by a definite time. He wants to make this promise, but he has still enough conscience to ask himself: "Is it not unlawful and inconsistent with duty to get out of a difficulty in this way?" Suppose, however, that he resolves to do so. The maxim of his action would then be expressed like this: "When I think myself in want of money, I will borrow money and promise to repay it, although I know I never can do so." Now this principle of self-love or one's own advantage may perhaps be consistent with my whole future welfare; but the question now is, "Is it right?" I change the suggestion of self-love into a universal law, and state the question like this: "How would it be if my maxim were a universal law?"
